title: The Circuit That Shouldn't Have Burned
featured_title: THE CIRCUIT THAT SHOULDN'T HAVE BURNED
subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students

case_dna.target_misconception: If resistance and current calculations are correct, the selected resistor must be suitable.
case_dna.why_plausible: Students often stop at Ohm's Law and do not compare operating power with the component's power rating.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: The circuit dissipates 72 W in a resistor rated for only 10 W.
case_dna.corrected_model: Correct circuit behavior and safe component selection are separate checks. Calculate operating power and compare it with rated capacity plus design margin.

problem_statement: A 12 V source is connected across a required 2 Ω load. The calculated and measured current is 6 A, but the resistor overheats and fails within seconds. Identify the missing engineering check, prove the root cause, and choose a safe correction.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The calculation is correct. It still failed.
facts: Calculated current: I = V/R = 6 A — checked twice
Result: resistor overheated and failed within seconds
gates.prompt: Something else has to be true — what was missed?
gates.cta: This doesn't add up — let's dig in

gates.label: Theory
gates.heading: Commit a theory before new evidence appears

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict, before we test it
gates.prompt: How much power (W) do you think the resistor was dissipating when it failed?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Run the experiment
gates.result: R4 overheats and fails. Actual power dissipation is 72 W.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Explain the gap
gates.prompt: Using P = I²R, calculate the actual power dissipated. I = 6 A, R = 2 Ω.

cards.text: Component spec sheet: resistor rated for 10 W maximum.
Wiring inspection: continuity and insulation normal. No fault found.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Redline the report
report: C1. Supply voltage measured at 12 V, within spec.
C2. Current calculated at 6 A using Ohm's Law, consistent with design.
C3. Since the current calculation checks out, the design was sound — the failure was likely a manufacturing defect.

evidence_choices.label: Supply voltage log — clean, no spikes
Wiring inspection — clean, no fault found
Power dissipation (72 W) exceeds rated capacity (10 W)

correction.template: The resistor failed because its power rating of {rating} W was exceeded by an actual dissipation of {dissipation} W — not a manufacturing defect.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Fix the design under the stated constraints

options.label: Specify a 2 Ω resistor with a higher power rating and safety margin
Add a fuse to limit current

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Independent transfer — no help this time
gates.prompt: A heater is connected to a constant-voltage source. Its resistance is cut in half. What happens to the power it dissipates?
gates.explanation: At constant voltage, P = V²/R. Halving R doubles P.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off as the engineer of record
gates.confirmation: I confirm this conclusion is supported by evidence, not assumption.

items.label: What broke it
items.value: 72 W operating dissipation exceeded the 10 W component rating.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: A correct current calculation does not guarantee an adequately rated component.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Always compare calculated power with rated capacity and appropriate margin.

seo.seo_title: Why a Resistor Burns Even When Ohm's Law Is Correct | FE Case E-017
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-017: a 12 V, 2 Ω circuit draws the correct 6 A but the resistor still burns. Diagnose the missed power-rating check.
seo.excerpt: A correct current calculation does not guarantee a safe resistor. Investigate why a 2 Ω resistor fails in a 12 V circuit even though Ohm's Law checks out.
seo.direct_answer: The resistor failed because its 10 W power rating was far below the 72 W it had to dissipate. Correct resistance and current values do not prove that a component is adequately rated.

faqs.q: Why can a resistor burn even when the resistance value is correct?
faqs.a: Because the resistor may be forced to dissipate more power than its wattage rating allows.

faqs.q: How much power does a 2 Ω resistor dissipate at 6 A?
What should an engineer check after calculating current?
faqs.a: Check operating power against the component's rated power and apply an appropriate design margin.
